item.title: Meet Anthropic’s sandbox-runtime: OS-Level Sandboxing for AI Agents, No Containers
item.abstract: In this article, we will discuss newly trending open sourced Anthropic’s sandbox-runtime (srt) , the OS-level sandbox behind Claude Code’s sandboxed bash tool. The Anthropic sandbox-runtime limits which files a process can touch and which hosts it can reach. It does this without spinning up a container. It is also not tied to Claude Code. Your own agents, local MCP servers and plain command-line programs can run inside it. Anthropic sandbox-runtime is an open-source tool that wraps any process in filesystem and network restrictions. You install it with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime , then prefix a command with srt . It works as a CLI and as a TypeScript library. srt uses each operating system’s own isolation primitives. Its restrictions cover the entire process tree, including scripts and subprocesses. Traffic leaves only through HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies running on the host. On Linux, those proxies sit behind Unix sockets bind-mounted into the sandbox. On macOS, the Seatbelt profile allows only one localhost port. The proxies then apply your domain allowlist and denylist. Anthropic team argues that 1 boundary without the other fails. Without network isolation, a prompt-injected agent could exfiltrate SSH keys. Without filesystem isolation, it could escape the sandbox and gain network access. srt’s defaults follow that logic. Reads are allowed everywhere unless denied. Writes are denied everywhere unless allowed. Network access is denied unless a domain is allowlisted. For an MCP server, change the command in .mcp.json from npx to srt . Pass the original command as arguments. Rules then live in ~/.srt-settings.json : For your own agent, the library exposes SandboxManager . Call initialize(config) to start the proxies. Then wrapWithSandbox() returns a wrapped command string you can spawn. Anthropic reports that sandboxing reduced permission prompts by 84% in internal Claude Code usage. That is a self-reported number, not an external benchmark. The target is approval fatigue. Developers who click “approve” all day stop reading what they approve. A fixed boundary lets the agent work freely inside it and ask only at the edge. Coding agents do more than edit files. They install dependencies, pull docs and call APIs. Make the allowlist too strict and npm install fails. Make it too loose and the sandbox protects little. srt ships several knobs for that middle ground: Check out the GitHub repo , the Anthropic engineering post and the Claude Code sandboxing docs . item.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open Small Language Model for Local Voice Agents, Game Characters and Robots
item.abstract: NVIDIA has just released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , an open small language model for fast conversational agents. It targets voice assistants, game NPCs and robot interfaces running locally on RTX, Jetson and Spark hardware. The model is post-trained from Google’s Gemma 4 E4B using reinforcement learning only. For developers, this is agent behavior in about 4GB of VRAM. That leaves room for speech and vision models. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B is a small language model from NVIDIA that powers local conversational agents. It combines natural dialogue with multi-turn tool calling. NVIDIA lists 3 target workloads: device and voice assistants, interactive characters, and embedded or industrial agents. The research report shows a Reachy Mini robot running on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB. In that demo, Cosmos 3 Edge handles vision while Bolt handles speech replies and tool calls. NVIDIA team also calls Bolt the third-generation small model for NVIDIA ACE game characters . Core features from the launch post : NVIDIA skipped supervised fine-tuning entirely. As per the research report , SFT improved tool calling but hurt Gemma’s conversational quality and verbosity. Instead, the research team used RLVR and RLHF through NeMo-RL and NeMo-Gym . Every training sample ran in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Each batch kept a 2:1 ratio of non-reasoning to reasoning samples. Length penalties in the GenRM environment stopped answers from growing during training. The datasets and the full recipe are public. For deployment, NVIDIA quantized the BF16 checkpoint to Q4_K_M with importance-matrix calibration. Calibration used about 1M tokens of RL rollouts. The release also ships a DFlash drafter for speculative decoding. On an RTX 5070, Bolt with DFlash reached 272.6 tokens/s. Gemma 4 E4B with its MTP drafter reached 225.9 tokens/s, so Bolt is 1.21x faster. NVIDIA grouped 21 benchmarks into 5 capability areas. All scores here are BF16, measured by NVIDIA in its own NeMo-Gym harness. Bolt led 15 of 21 rows in reasoning mode. NVIDIA also reports roughly 40% higher average scores than Nemotron 3 Nano 4B. It claims up to 80% fewer output tokens in reasoning-enabled comparisons. Separately, Scale Labs ranked Bolt first among small models on MultiChallenge at 56.03%, per an X post . Bolt does not win everywhere. Qwen3.5-4B leads on Tau2-Bench (75.1 vs 55.1) and RULER 64K (95.1 vs 87.0). It also leads LongBench v2 (59.9 vs 50.5) and BFCL-v3 (70.9 vs 68.5). Gemma 4 E4B keeps a narrow edge on EQ-Bench v3 (41.1 vs 39.4). *Benchmark rows are NVIDIA-measured BF16 scores from the Bolt launch post . Vendor-reported scores differ. NVIDIA measured the Q4_K_M build with llama.cpp at batch size 1. The figures below use 3K input and 50 output tokens. The ‘4GB’ label describes a target memory envelope, not the file size. The Q4_K_M GGUF on Hugging Face is 6.18 GB. Bolt is available on Hugging Face , Ollama , LM Studio, Unsloth and Jetson AI Lab . It also ships as an NVIDIA NIM and through the In-Game Inferencing SDK . Check out the technical report , GGUF model , BF16 model and training recipe . item.title: Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro: A 2.8T Total/104B Active Params (MoE) Model with 1M Context
item.abstract: Moonshot AI has just released Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in its K3.1 series. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3T-class open-weight* model with a 1-million-token context window. Moonshot team positions it against the strongest proprietary models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. For developers, it is cheaper API pricing than K3 and open weights yet not available. *open weights are expected to release in November 2026 . Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with much larger post-training compute. Moonshot team ran joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains. To support this, the Moonshot team optimized the RL framework, long-context inference, sandbox infrastructure and rollout scheduling. The base K3 architecture uses Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). It activates 16 of 896 experts through a Stable LatentMoE framework. The model accepts text, images and video through the API, per the quickstart docs . Moonshot team also shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed . According to the official Moonshot blog, it runs 2 to 3x faster . All numbers below are self-reported by Moonshot at max reasoning effort, mostly with the Claude Code harness. Moonshot removed cyber-related data from mid-training and RL for the open-weight release. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, an unfiltered checkpoint solved 90.5% at pass@3. The shipped K3.1 Pro solves 81.0%. Moonshot says it stays behind frontier proprietary models on offensive cyber tasks. The model is live on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API . The API IDs are kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed . The endpoint is OpenAI-compatible. Pricing for K3.1 Pro is $2.00 input and $10.00 output per million tokens. Cache hits cost $0.20. Highspeed costs $4.00 input and $20.00 output. K3 itself was priced at $3.00 and $15.00. item.title: Kyutai CADRE: Video Autoencoders That Cut World Model Lag Below 230 ms
item.abstract: Kyutai has released CADRE , open causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. The Kyutai CADRE video autoencoder targets one problem: action lag. Many world models borrow autoencoders from text-to-video generators. Those autoencoders pack many frames into one latent, so every action waits. Per the research paper , CADRE world models run at 20 fps on 1 H100 and react within 230 ms. CADRE is a family of video autoencoders from Kyutai built for action-conditioned world models. A world model generates in the autoencoder’s latent space. So the autoencoder’s compression sets both cost per frame and action delay. Compression is written τ×s×s. τ is frames per latent, and s is the spatial factor. The research gives the latency as τ/f plus generation and decode time. At τ = 8 and 20 fps, the chunk alone adds 400 ms. Humans notice their own movement lagging beyond about 230 ms. The encoder reuses the MIRA recipe. A frozen DINOv3 extracts per-patch features from each frame. One trained 3D convolution then compresses them into a 64-channel latent. Only this bottleneck changes between the 7 members. The decoder is a causal diffusion transformer with 24 blocks. It streams chunk by chunk. Progressive self-distillation teaches it to decode in 1 or 2 steps. This happens in a single training stage, without an adversarial loss. The autoencoders train on 23 public video sources, about 76k hours. The mix spans web, robot, driving and game video. Kyutai trained the same 1.2B causal diffusion transformer on each autoencoder. It used 4 environments: robot manipulation (ABC), human manipulation (EgoDex), driving (PhysicalAI AV) and indoor navigation (RealEstate10K). Each model sees 2 s of real video, then generates 4.8 s. Scores cover image quality (FID), motion quality (FVD) and action following (ARR). ARR uses a frozen inverse dynamics probe. An ARR of 1 matches real video. On one H100, CADRE-2×32×32 reacts in 185 ms and sustains 23.4 fps with 1 decoding step. The Wan 2.2 autoencoder needs 317 ms, LTX-2 492 ms and Cosmos 605 ms. DC-AE is faster at 118 ms but frame-by-frame. The gap is widest with a moving camera. In driving, Wan 2.2 FVD reaches 599.7 and LTX-2 913.3. In indoor navigation, LTX-2 ARR falls to 0.04. Against the retrained MIRA decoder, the 1-step diffusion decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5×. Latency, fpsA, FVD, ARR and PSNR: CADRE paper , Tables 4, 6 and 7. CADRE uses 1 decoding step. All figures are self-reported by Kyutai. CADRE does not win everywhere. In robot manipulation, Cosmos posts an FVD of 39.5 against 47.6 for the best 1-step CADRE. At the fast end, DC-AE beats CADRE-1×48×48 in manipulation. Wan 2.2 also reconstructs held-out video far better, at 35.02 dB PSNR. Kyutai team argues reconstruction does not predict rollouts. Wan 2.2 ranks last on indoor rollout FVD. Long latents leave visible seams between chunks. At τ = 8, boundary excess reaches 1.6 to 1.8 across environments. CADRE-4×24×24 is an outlier in navigation, with FVD 403 in driving. Each world model covers one environment at 288×512. Whether findings transfer to generalist models remains open. The code is MIT licensed. Weights on Hugging Face are CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use is excluded. The release covers 7 autoencoders, 4 longer-trained multi-resolution versions and 4 world models on CADRE-2×16×16. A live demo lets you drive them by keyboard. item.title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
item.abstract: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

item.title: Stateful Agentic Engineering Copilots with Letta: Core Memory, Shared State, Semantic Retrieval, Custom Tools, Streaming, and Portable Agent Workflows
item.abstract: In this tutorial, we build a stateful engineering copilot with Letta that demonstrates how agentic memory extends beyond conventional prompt-based conversations. We begin by creating inspectable core memory blocks that the agent can autonomously update, then expose those blocks for programmatic state synchronization and shared access across multiple agents. We further extend the architecture with archival vector memory for semantic retrieval, a custom server-side tool for deterministic risk estimation, streaming for observing agent execution, server-side message history for persistent conversations, and .af export for portability. Together, these components demonstrate a practical memory architecture in which persistent state, retrieval, tools, multi-agent collaboration, and execution traces work as an integrated agentic system. We set up the Letta client, install the SDK, and add compatibility helpers that handle API variations across Letta versions. We dynamically select an available model and create a stateful engineering copilot with structured core memory blocks. We then inspect the initial memory state to establish the agent’s persistent context. We demonstrate self-editing memory by providing the copilot with durable information about the engineer, project, decisions, and known failure modes. We also update project state directly from application code and create shared read-only and writable blocks for multi-agent collaboration. We then connect a reviewer agent to the shared memory and observe how both agents exchange persistent working context. We populate archival memory with tagged engineering knowledge and use semantic search to retrieve relevant information without relying on exact keyword matches. We then allow the agent to query this archival knowledge autonomously when answering an operational question. Finally, we create and attach a custom server-side release-risk tool so the agent can perform deterministic calculations and record the resulting decision in memory. We use Letta’s streaming interface to observe reasoning, tool calls, and assistant responses as the agent executes a task. We then inspect server-side conversation history to verify that the interaction state persists independently of the local Python process. We also demonstrate how the agent can be reconnected from a fresh process using only its persistent identifier. We export the complete agent state to an .af file, providing a portable representation of the agent’s memory, tools, and conversation state. We then include optional cleanup logic that removes the agents and shared blocks created during the tutorial. We finish by displaying the persistent agent identifiers and the Letta ADE location for further inspection. In conclusion, we now have a complete view of how Letta supports persistent, inspectable agent workflows rather than treating every interaction as an isolated prompt. We saw how core memory maintains high-value state in context, archival memory provides scalable retrieval, shared and read-only blocks coordinate multiple agents, and application code can directly synchronize external state. We also used custom tools and streaming to extend and observe agent behavior while server-side history and agent export provide persistence and portability. Through this workflow, we established a practical foundation for building engineering copilots that continuously retain context, reason over accumulated knowledge, collaborate across agents, and operate with explicit, controllable memory. item.title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
item.abstract: Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack. Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year . Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has. We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence. https://t.co/r0qFLdvd6c — jack (@jack) October 23, 2026 Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags. “Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post . The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired. We made the first AI model you can have a realistic conversation with that was trained entirely on speech! Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that you can run on consumer GPUs. This is a GPT3 moment for speech. pic.twitter.com/XVD8sSyJn8 — Ragavan Thurairatnam (@RagavanThurair) October 23, 2026 In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down. Dessa=full-duplex speech model vs Human=me, https://t.co/1eI6QFHo1w pic.twitter.com/zlZfxH2BA5 — Aydin Polat (@AydinPolatDessa) October 23, 2026 Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant. For the love of the game. Watch Cara play a guessing game with Dessa. The model guesses the first one right straight away, and the second doesn’t take long either. https://t.co/FDmoXNPpIh pic.twitter.com/I9f8saduEA — Block (@blocks) October 23, 2026 The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end. Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering . But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

item.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
item.abstract: On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access. The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post . OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models. The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible. Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.” “In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.” The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded. Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach. To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.” Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

item.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
item.abstract: AI News OpenAI OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found. AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found. by Emma Roth Oct 23, 2026, 9:11 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of The AI Superintelligence Slowdown see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday , OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.” OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September , after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies , or swarm obscure websites . On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says. Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.” In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects . item.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
item.abstract: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots. There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them. “ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.” SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment. Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions. “It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics. “If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said. Previous research has raised similar concerns. The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing. The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt. Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%. GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.) The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy. ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans. The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote. Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72. “If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said. One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights. Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat. When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.” The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine. Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections. In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. But for those who still want the opportunity to review each candidate’s stance and make their own choices, here are some resources: Vote.gov League of Women Voters’ vote411.org Ballotpedia VoteSmart FEC.gov and OpenSecrets State and county election offices Candidates’ websites and local news

item.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
item.abstract: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy Image Credits: Ask Proxy Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy Image Credits: Caddy Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma Image Credits: Comma Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot Image Credits: Fambot Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk Image Credits: Folk Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct Image Credits: Instinct Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . The company remains in private beta. Iris Image Credits: Iris Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request. Martin Image Credits: Martin Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick Image Credits: Maverick Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use. It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

item.title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
item.abstract:
Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell. Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) blast radius affects many libraries & apps using HTTPs. Buckle up. Written by Dania Durnas Published on: Oct 23, 2026 Last updated on: Oct 24, 2026 TL;DR ⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well. On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available. Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available. Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli , Python , C++ , NodeJS , bun , Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default. Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here . ‍ What is Brotli? Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. What is CVE-2026-111497? CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library. A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code. OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses. The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update. ‍ You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet. ‍ You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel. Python C++ Libbrotil NodeJS As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497 For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library: Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 , or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line. Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later . For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 . Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later , wherever installed. curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1 , a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build. Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later . Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun. Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8 , or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported. Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2 . Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life. Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number. Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider. Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components. ‍ Fixed releases, reviewed October 23, 2026 Project Patch status Fixed versions Notes Node.js Patch available 22.23.4 · 24.22.1 · 26.12.1 Use a supported release line. Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late. Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header. item.title: UUIDv7: Timestamps aren’t time-ordered and other oddities
item.abstract:
Built on Shards of Silicon This post is part of a collection on UUIDs . I’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird. Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits: monotonically increasing IDs a helpful timestamp of when the object was created; and unguessable IDs But none of these properties are strictly held.
Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees.
The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance.
I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable ,
so this post explores the other properties. Is the timestamp useful? Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations.
If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index. Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time.
The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”. RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock.
This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy.
In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large. Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1 This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1 … implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2 Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem.
If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future.
Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits.
A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems.
This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section. Example: Python uuid.uuid7() One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7.
The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows.
Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount. Here’s a simple example: import uuid
from datetime import datetime # Prime the generator with the current time
t = uuid.uuid7().time
now = datetime.now()
delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
print("Initial delta: ", delta)
# Ask the user to change the time
input("Set clock back one hour") while True: for _ in range(100000): uuid.uuid7() t = uuid.uuid7().time now = datetime.now() delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds() print("New delta: ", delta) Which gives: $ uv run --python 3.14 main.py
Initial delta: -0.000748
Set clock back one hour
New delta: 3695.277581
New delta: 3795.042411
New delta: 3894.80756
New delta: 3994.573106
^C We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp.
But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound.
At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect. The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”.
I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations.
Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior.
There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments. Is leaking a timestamp harmful? Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp. It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters.
One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp. This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments.
Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it.
If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata. Are UUIDv7s monotonic? This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough.
Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements. When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered.
This was proven impossible back in the 1970s ,
and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision.
Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is.
Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering. Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is. For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted.
It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them.
At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect. But even on a single node, using a single implementation, UUIDv7 IDs are not strictly monotonic.
The easiest way to get out-of-order UUIDv7 IDs is to use an implementation that uses a millisecond timestamp without a counter.
This approach trivially generates out-of-order IDs inside a small for loop . So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing.
Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable. In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful.
So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet.
Just be wary of what assumptions you have. Restarting a UUIDv7 generator The RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards.
Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed. We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used.
To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart. I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage.
So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards. Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates .

item.title: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
item.abstract:
Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology Posted on October 24, 2026 by steve blank I’ve been in London for the last month and have heard policymakers react to the wake up call Elon Musk just delivered. The decision of the U.S. to shut off intelligence and throttle the military version of Starlink called Starshield to Ukraine may have been a blip in the news in the US, but it has sent tremors across Europe. For years doomsayers in the UK and Europe were worried about the U.S. having a kill switch in weapon systems and critical commercial technology that could disconnect them at will. Most people, including me, thought that it was a paranoid fantasy. Until it happened. Seemingly on a whim of a single individual, ( according to the Wall Street Journal ) Elon Musk personally ordered the restrictions, and the effect was to tilt Russia’s war against Ukraine in favor of the Russians. This wasn’t an articulated U.S. foreign policy nor was it an announced act of the U.S. government. From news accounts it appears to have been a personal decision of an American CEO acting unilaterally. Blowback For whatever reason, whether it was to satisfy a request from the White House or some personal animosity to the Ukrainians, from Europe’s perspective, that’s almost beside the point. An American company operating critical military infrastructure was able to degrade the capability of an American partner in the middle of a war. Without warning. The message heard loud and clear here in Europe was that the U.S. is an unreliable security and technology partner willing to throw any partner under the bus, at any time, for any reason . The conversations I’ve heard have included, “what happens if other U.S. CEOs – Microsoft, OpenAI or Anthropic, Oracle, Palantir, or Google – decide to restrict/limit or deny access to their products? What capabilities would Europe lose if enterprise software and/or AI across Europe goes dark?” This was a laughable scenario until this week. To a lot of European decision makers, it is no longer outside the realm of possibility. The lesson that was brought home was that no nation, Europe or elsewhere, can continue to outsource its national sovereignty and security by depending solely on US data systems or intelligence. Unintended Consequences Besides the political ramifications, the business ones are going to come home to roost. If every U.S. vendor is now a kill-switch risk, the allied market for that whole ecosystem shrinks. As it sinks into the European countries that the U.S, can simply shut off any technology, over time they will find and build alternatives. In the years ahead, this may cost American companies tens if not hundreds of billions of lost revenue. Europe has been debating digital sovereignty for years. Up to this year, the idea of cloning the capabilities of the best U.S. products seemed like an insurmountable problem. And some, like low-cost access to space, still are. But today AI collapses the cost of creating sovereign software at exactly the time that geopolitical risk is increasing customers’ willingness to switch. AI makes recreating the features, functions and compatibility of Microsoft Office, Oracle, Salesforce, Palantir, Anduril, et al. within reach. AI puts it well within the capabilities of most nations. The U.S. spent decades establishing itself as the world’s indispensable technology supplier. A substantial part of that advantage depended on customers believing American technology would remain reliable and available. Going forward a U.S. founder selling into European defense or government now needs an answer to “who holds the switch” before the first meeting; and European founders just got sovereignty as a sellable feature. What was done in a fit of pique will cost the U.S. both leadership and jobs. Filed under: National Security , Teaching |
